newsitem.title: CUBA: Pope's envoy seeks more space for church in Cuba.
newsitem.headline: Pope's envoy seeks more space for church in Cuba.

text.p: Visiting Vatican Foreign Minister Jean Louis Tauran called on Sunday for the Roman Catholic Church to be allowed a more public role in communist-ruled Cuba.
The church had to enjoy a wider space than just the formal right to practise religion, he said, adding that to reduce it to this role was to "mutilate faith."

Speaking at a mass in a packed Havana church, Tauran also said he was opeful that Pope John Paul will visit the island. Such a visit, he said, should "set the seal on a climate of religious freedom and confidence (in Cuba)".

Tauran is the first Vatican foreign minister to be invited to Cuba by the government and his visit, which began Friday, comes at a time of marked improvement in relations between the authorities and the church. But Tauran made clear the Vatican felt relations could improve further.

Tauran's visit comes amid speculation Cuban President Fidel Castro may meet the pontiff if he travels to Rome for a summit on food being organised by the U.N.'s Food and Agriculture Organisation from November 13 to 17. Diplomatic sources in Rome have said if Castro does meet the pope he will probably invite him to Cuba, likely next year.

Tauran, who is likely to meet Castro during his five-day stay in Cuba, said the Roman Catholic church in Cuba was growing "amid trials and hope." The fact it was enjoying what he called a "springtime" of renovation meant it was facing new challenges, he added.

On relations between church and state, Tauran said there should be a "healthy cooperation." The church was independent of politics but it served the same aim of political leaders, that of serving society, he said.
Since the church wanted only to serve, it "asks for the necessary spaces of freedom and service," he said.
Tauran gave as one example of the church's needs was a shortage of clergy. He said there was a need for more Cuban clergy and also for more foreigners, he said.

Foreigners should be allowed in without delay, he said, in a reference to a feeling in church circles that the government holds up visas for foreign priests and nuns going to join the current body of some 250 priests and 450 nuns in the country.

Tauran said the church charity Caritas should be able to help the needy without obstacles and that help should not be just material but also social. Caritas should be allowed to work in areas such as schools, hospitals and jails, he said.

Sunday's service was attended by Cuba's Cardinal Jaime Ortega, Cuban bishops and priests, Cuban officials including deputy foreign minister Isabel Allende and members of the diplomatic corps in Havana, as well as ordinary Cubans.
Those who could not squeeze into the building stood in a park outside watching the service on a screen on a wall.
Tauran Saturday met Foreign Minister Roberto Robaina and parliamentary president Ricardo Alarcon, before travelling to the western city of Pinar del Rio for a mass.
He was likely to meet Castro before leaving Tuesday, though the meeting has not been announced in advance, as is usual with the Cuban leader.

Cuban authorities have moved in recent years to improve ties with Christian churches, strained after Castro's 1959 revolution. But tensions with the Catholic Church persisted, mainly over calls by the bishops for political change.
However there has been a clear improvement in recent months. Cardinal Ortega said in September that comments on religion in a Communist Party document were encouraging.
